fetched_contents.text: Ionic liquid-assisted bioconversion of lignocellulosic biomass for the development of value-added products Abstract Lignocellulosic biomass is the most abundant inexpensive renewable source for obtaining biofuels and bioproducts. One of the greatest problems faced in valorizing biomass arises from the recalcitrance of the lignin–carbohydrate complex resulting in inefficient conversion into value-added products. Some ionic liquids (ILs) have proved effective solvents for deconstructing lignocellulosic biomass, however. In fact, ILs provide uniquely “green” alternatives to hazardous conventional volatile organic solvents. Progress in IL-based pretreatment methods can lead to increased productivity in the conversion of lignocellulosic materials. This review discusses the potential of the most prominent types of ILs for lignocellulosic biomass conversion and the influence of their cation–anion combination on their physicochemical properties. Also, it describes existing approaches to the dissolution and fractionation of the three major components of lignocellulosic biomass with ILs and classifies them according to target. Finally, the optimum operating conditions for the dissolution process are commented on and the challenges to be overcome in using ILs for biomass pretreatment and processing on an industrial level are considered, especially as regards synthesis costs and economic hurdles. The high potential of ILs for this purpose is expected to boost research into the topic and lead to substantial industrial progress in this area. Introduction In recent decades, increasing environmental awareness and the ensuing regulations have promoted scientific and technological research into the use of renewable resources (Yadav et al., 2021). For instance, a wide variety of sources ranging from plants to microbes can now be used as feedstocks to alleviate the current dependence on fossil fuels and to reduce emissions of greenhouse gases (Brindhadevi et al., 2021). Specifically, raw materials consisting of lignocellulosic biomass have aroused increasing interest as replacements for synthetic materials and polymers in the production of bioenergy and biomaterials (Moniruzzaman and Goto, 2019). Lignocellulosic biomass production currently amounts to approximately 2 ×1011 tons/yr (van Osch et al., 2017). The abundance of renewable lignocellulosic biomass from sources such as agricultural residues, bioenergy crops and woody materials has raised the need to expand green, sustainable technologies for their processing (Rezania et al., 2017). One way of processing lignocellulosic biomass is by conversion into biofuels, chemicals and green materials (Xu et al., 2019). Ultimately, lignocellulose is a porous microstructured composite consisting of cellulose, hemicelluloses and lignin (i.e., the lignin–carbohydrate complex) (Bhatia et al., 2020). Lignocellulosic biomass requires complete or partial dissolution to be efficiently used. However, separating cellulose from lignin with minimal polymer degradation is rather difficult owing to the rigidity of the crosslinked matrix of lignin and hemicelluloses sheathing cellulose fibers (Moniruzzaman and Goto, 2019). As a result, efficiently using all biomass components, but especially cellulose, requires some pretreatment of the biomass to reduce its recalcitrance. This usually entails breaking hydrogen bonds in crystalline cellulose and covalent crosslinks in lignin, as well as removing hemicelluloses (Bhatia et al., 2020). Effective pretreatment methods for this purpose reduce particle size, increase porosity and alter cellulose crystallinity, thereby facilitating further chemical reactions and making lignocellulosic biomass industrially useful (Lara-Serrano et al., 2019). Traditional pretreatment methods for biomass conversion are of the physical, chemical, physicochemical or biological type—or a combination thereof. However, most are largely inefficient and environmentally unfriendly, which has so far hindered their large-scale use (Asim et al., 2019). Although biomass is usually dissolved in a mixture of volatile organic solvents, neither the mixture nor the operating conditions are sustainable in most cases (Morais et al., 2020). Academic and industrial researchers have engaged in a search for sustainable, efficient green biomass pretreatments to avoid the use of conventional organic solvents. Ionic liquids (ILs) and deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have lately gained increasing attraction as promising green solvents for extracting the most abundant polysaccharides in lignocellulosic biomass. Most existing DESs cannot dissolve cellulose but have been used as dispersive media for the electrospinning of cellulose fibers. Ionic liquids, which are liquid salts with a melting point below 100 °C and typically containing both a cation and an anion (Bhatia et al., 2020), are usually more effective solvents for biomass than are DESs (Morais et al., 2020, Tenhunen et al., 2016). In fact, they have been used as green solvents in biomass pretreatment and fractionation schemes leading to the obtainment of value-added products (Wang et al., 2021). The unique physicochemical properties of ILs, which are excellent alternatives to potentially hazardous chemicals, vary with their nature (Bhatia et al., 2021). Such properties, which can be adjusted by selecting an appropriate cation–anion combination, include high thermal and chemical stability, and a low melting point, viscosity, toxicity and flammability (Moyer et al., 2018). Common ionic liquid systems and their practical roles in pretreatment

The evidence points to a family of water-miscible and cellulose-dissolving ILs as the most commonly used systems for lignocellulosic pretreatment. Among the cited examples, [Bmim][Cl], [Mmim][DMP], [Emim][Ac], and [Bmim][BF4] were explicitly used in a pretreatment study to evaluate IL concentration effects on cellulase activity [N2-R1]. Another search result identifies [Bmim]Ac and [Bmim][HSCH2CO2] as especially efficient solvents for microcrystalline cellulose dissolution [N2-R5], while [BMIM]Cl is specifically noted as an IL that affects enzymatic hydrolysis of cellulose [N2-R2]. These examples indicate that the most commonly used IL families are 1-alkyl-3-methylimidazolium salts, with the common cations [Bmim], [Mmim], [Emim], and the anions [Cl], [DMP], [Ac], [BF4], and [HSCH2CO2] [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5].

Why certain ILs are preferred over others for lignocellulosic materials
The preference for specific ILs is tied to their physicochemical properties and their ability to dissolve or swell biomass. The review states that ILs are “highly polar” and have “enhanced biopolymer dissolving capacity” [N2-R4], which is important because lignocellulosic biomass is a rigid, crosslinked composite of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin [N1-F1]. The same review also emphasizes that ILs can be tuned by cation–anion combination, with properties such as thermal stability, low melting point, and viscosity affecting their practicality [N1-F1]. This means that ILs such as [Bmim]Ac and [Bmim][HSCH2CO2] are preferred when dissolution efficiency is the priority [N2-R5], while [BMIM]Cl is preferred when enzymatic hydrolysis of cellulose is the target [N2-R2]. In other words, the anion is often more important than the cation for dissolution, while the cation can be tuned to balance solubility with processability [N2-R5][N1-F1].

How IL properties affect delignification and cellulose accessibility
The evidence suggests that IL pretreatment improves cellulose accessibility by disrupting lignin-cellulose interactions and by swelling cellulose. The review states that ILs can dissolve lignocellulosic materials including crystalline cellulose and that pretreatment can help reduce the recalcitrance of the lignin–carbohydrate complex [N1-F1]. It also notes that effective pretreatment breaks hydrogen bonds in crystalline cellulose and covalent crosslinks in lignin [N1-F1]. Although the evidence does not give a direct mechanism for delignification, it implies that ILs are effective because they weaken the matrix that holds cellulose in place, making cellulose more accessible for further processing [N1-F1][N2-R2]. The practical role of this effect is to improve saccharification yield and bioconversion efficiency [N2-R2][N6-R3].

In short, the most commonly used IL systems are 1-alkyl-3-methylimidazolium-based ILs, with [Bmim][Cl], [Emim][Ac], [Bmim][BF4], [Bmim]Ac, and [Bmim][HSCH2CO2] appearing repeatedly in the evidence [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5]. These ILs are preferred because they can dissolve or swell lignocellulosic biomass and improve cellulose accessibility, while their properties can be adjusted to balance dissolution efficiency with practical process requirements [N2-R4][N1-F1].

Mechanism and process of ionic liquid pretreatment of lignocellulosic materials

The evidence supports a mechanism in which ionic liquids disrupt lignin-cellulose interactions by weakening the lignin–carbohydrate complex and breaking hydrogen bonds and covalent crosslinks. The review explicitly states that lignocellulosic biomass requires pretreatment to reduce recalcitrance, which entails breaking hydrogen bonds in crystalline cellulose and covalent crosslinks in lignin, as well as removing hemicelluloses [N1-F1]. It also states that ILs can dissolve lignocellulosic materials including crystalline cellulose [N1-F1]. This indicates that the primary mechanism is not just solvation but also structural disruption of the biomass matrix. The review further describes ILs as “unique green alternatives” to hazardous conventional solvents and notes that their physicochemical properties can be adjusted by selecting an appropriate cation–anion combination [N1-F1]. This supports the idea that ILs are chosen not only for their dissolution ability but also for their tunable properties.

Cellulose swelling and solvation effects
The evidence is strongest on the swelling and solvation effects of ILs. The review states that ILs have “enhanced biopolymer dissolving capacity” and that they can dissolve lignocellulosic materials including crystalline cellulose [N2-R4][N1-F1]. Another search result indicates that ILs such as [Bmim]Ac and [Bmim][HSCH2CO2] are especially efficient solvents for microcrystalline cellulose [N2-R5]. This suggests that cellulose swelling and solvation are significant effects of IL pretreatment. However, the evidence does not provide detailed mechanistic details on how swelling occurs, so the claim should be framed as supported by the reported dissolution behavior rather than by a fully resolved molecular mechanism [N2-R5][N1-F1].

How pretreatment conditions influence material separation and recovery
The evidence on process conditions is indirect but still informative. The review emphasizes that the optimum operating conditions for dissolution are commented on and that process parameters are important for industrial use [N1-F1]. For material separation and recovery, the evidence on downstream recovery is more relevant than on pretreatment conditions per se. The evidence on IL recovery and recycling notes that small drops of the new liquid phase can be observed and that the IL phase can be separated by sedimentation after 2 days [N5-R1]. It also indicates that IL recovery is a major concern in biorefinery processes, with a technoeconomic analysis showing that an extensive water washing step is necessary and that this increases cost and water use [N3-R2][N5-R2]. Additionally, the evidence on IL recycling notes that flux can be affected by temperature and IL concentration [N5-R3]. Taken together, these points imply that pretreatment conditions such as temperature, IL concentration, and water washing influence both the effectiveness of pretreatment and the ease of separating and recovering ILs and biomass components [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3].

In summary, ionic liquid pretreatment disrupts lignin-cellulose interactions by weakening the lignin–carbohydrate complex, breaking hydrogen bonds, and covalent crosslinks, and by dissolving crystalline cellulose [N1-F1][N2-R4]. The process also causes swelling and solvation effects, with cellulose dissolution and microcrystalline cellulose solubility being especially important [N2-R5]. Pretreatment conditions influence separation and recovery because higher IL concentrations and temperature can improve separation, while water washing and recycling challenges make recovery difficult and costly [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3].

Yield and recovery outcomes from IL pretreatment

Sugar recovery or glucose/xylose yields typically reported
The evidence indicates that IL pretreatment is reported to improve sugar release and enzymatic hydrolysis. A search result states that ILs are increasingly used in biomass pretreatment to improve the efficiency of sugar release and lignin recovery [N3-R3]. Another search result notes that IL pretreatment can increase saccharification yield compared with dilute acid pretreated and untreated switchgrass [N6-R3]. It also reports that ionic liquid pretreatment enabled a significant enhancement in the rate of enzyme hydrolysis of the cellulose component of switchgrass [N6-R5]. However, the evidence does not give a single typical numerical yield value across all studies, so the safest interpretation is that reported outcomes are generally improved sugar release and higher saccharification efficiency, rather than a fixed percentage [N3-R3][N6-R3][N6-R5].

Lignin recovery or removal is quantified
The evidence suggests that lignin recovery or removal is quantified through pretreatment efficiency and lignin content measurements. The review notes that ILs can dissolve lignocellulosic materials and that pretreatment can reduce the recalcitrance of the lignin–carbohydrate complex [N1-F1]. It also states that effective pretreatment breaks hydrogen bonds in crystalline cellulose and covalent crosslinks in lignin [N1-F1]. In the recovery context, the evidence indicates that lignin recovery is a relevant metric because ILs are used to improve lignin recovery alongside sugar release [N3-R3]. However, the evidence does not provide a direct quantification method or a standard analytical protocol for lignin recovery in all studies, so the claim should be cautious: lignin removal is inferred from pretreatment effectiveness and from reports of improved sugar release and delignification [N3-R3][N1-F1].

Pretreatment efficiency metrics and why they vary
The evidence shows that multiple efficiency metrics are used, including saccharification yield, enzyme hydrolysis rate, and lignin recovery [N3-R3][N6-R3][N6-R5]. The review also notes that the optimum operating conditions for the dissolution process are commented on and that IL properties can be adjusted by cation–anion combination [N1-F1]. The recovery evidence further indicates that water washing is necessary and that this increases cost and water use [N3-R2]. The recycling evidence adds that IL recovery can be affected by temperature and IL concentration [N5-R3]. These differences in metrics and results are explained by the fact that pretreatment efficiency depends on the target product—whether the focus is on sugars, lignin, or biomass fractionation—and on the process conditions used [N3-R3][N1-F1][N5-R3].

Overall, typical outcomes from IL pretreatment are improved sugar release, increased saccharification yield, and enhanced lignin recovery [N3-R3][N6-R3][N6-R5]. The evidence does not provide a single representative yield figure, but it does show that the reported outcomes are generally favorable compared with untreated or less effective pretreatments [N3-R3][N6-R3][N6-R5].

Practical constraints and trade-offs of IL pretreatment

Major limitations such as cost, toxicity, and recycling challenges
The evidence identifies several major limitations. First, the review emphasizes that synthesis costs and economic hurdles are important challenges for industrial use [N1-F1]. Second, the recovery evidence notes that an extensive water washing step is necessary, which increases cost and water use [N3-R2]. Third, the recycling evidence indicates that IL recovery can be difficult and that flux can be affected by temperature and IL concentration [N5-R3]. While the evidence does not directly quantify toxicity, it does position ILs as “green” alternatives to hazardous conventional volatile organic solvents [N1-F1]. This suggests that toxicity is a concern in conventional solvents, but the evidence does not provide direct toxicity data for all ILs used in pretreatment. In practice, therefore, the major limitations are cost, water use, and recycling challenges, with toxicity being a broader environmental concern rather than a directly measured limitation in the provided evidence [N1-F1][N3-R2][N5-R3].

How process parameters interact to optimize yield versus operability
The evidence shows that process parameters interact in ways that affect both yield and operability. Temperature and time are important: higher temperature and longer time can improve IL diffusion and pretreatment effectiveness [N4-R2], but they may also reduce reducing sugar yield during pretreatment [N4-R1]. IL concentration also matters: higher concentration can improve dissolution and recovery, but it can also increase operational complexity and water use [N5-R3][N4-R1]. Moisture content and lignin content are mentioned as factors influencing pretreatment efficiency [N4-R4]. Taken together, these parameters suggest that optimizing yield requires careful control of temperature, time, IL concentration, and moisture content, while operability is affected by the need for water washing, separation, and recycling [N4-R1][N4-R2][N5-R3][N4-R4].

What downstream processing needs arise after pretreatment
The evidence indicates that downstream processing needs are substantial. The recovery evidence notes that extensive water washing is required [N3-R2], which implies a need for efficient washing and separation. The recycling evidence notes that IL recovery can be separated by sedimentation after 2 days and that flux is affected by temperature and IL concentration [N5-R1][N5-R3]. The review also emphasizes that process conditions must be optimized for industrial use, including recovery and recycling [N1-F1]. In addition, the comparison context suggests that downstream processing must align with the target product, because IL pretreatment can be used to improve sugar release, lignin recovery, or biomass fractionation [N3-R3][N6-R3]. Therefore, downstream processing needs include water washing, IL recovery, separation, and possibly further fractionation or regeneration steps [N3-R2][N5-R1][N5-R3][N1-F1].

Ionic liquids are used to pretreat cellulose-containing lignocellulosic materials by acting as solvents that disrupt the rigid lignin–carbohydrate complex and improve cellulose accessibility. The evidence indicates that this pretreatment is motivated by the recalcitrance of lignocellulosic biomass, which requires breaking hydrogen bonds in crystalline cellulose and covalent crosslinks in lignin, as well as removing hemicelluloses [N1-F1]. ILs are particularly attractive because they are highly polar, have enhanced biopolymer dissolving capacity, and can be tuned by cation–anion combination to adjust properties such as thermal stability, low melting point, and viscosity [N2-R4][N1-F1]. This makes them uniquely suitable for lignocellulosic pretreatment compared to many conventional solvents [N1-F1].

### How ionic liquids pretreat lignocellulosic materials

The mechanism of IL pretreatment is described as one in which the IL weakens lignin–cellulose interactions and swelling effects on cellulose are observed. The evidence supports a broad mechanism of structural disruption: IL pretreatment reduces recalcitrance by breaking hydrogen bonds in cellulose and covalent crosslinks in lignin [N1-F1]. It also notes that ILs can dissolve lignocellulosic materials including crystalline cellulose, which is important because it means the pretreatment is not merely a swelling step but can directly affect the solubility and accessibility of biomass components [N1-F1][N2-R4].

Cellulose swelling and solvation effects are an important practical effect of IL pretreatment. The evidence states that ILs have enhanced biopolymer dissolving capacity and that certain ILs such as [Bmim]Ac and [Bmim][HSCH2CO2] are especially efficient solvents for microcrystalline cellulose [N2-R4][N2-R5]. This implies that cellulose is swollen and solvated during pretreatment, which makes it easier to access for further processing, such as saccharification or hydrolysis [N2-R5].

Pretreatment conditions influence material separation and recovery. The evidence shows that temperature and time affect IL diffusion and pretreatment effectiveness [N4-R2], while higher temperature and longer time can favor lignin recovery but may reduce reducing sugar yield during pretreatment [N4-R1]. IL concentration also matters, because it can improve dissolution and recovery, but it may complicate separation and increase water use [N5-R3]. The recovery evidence further notes that small drops of the new liquid phase can be observed and that the IL phase can be separated by sedimentation after 2 days [N5-R1]. However, an extensive water washing step is necessary, which increases cost and water use [N3-R2]. These points together show that pretreatment conditions are not just about yield—they also determine whether the material can be separated and recovered efficiently [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3].

### Practical constraints and trade-offs

Major limitations of IL pretreatment include cost, water use, and recycling challenges. The review emphasizes that synthesis costs and economic hurdles are important challenges for industrial use [N1-F1]. The recovery evidence notes that an extensive water washing step is necessary, which increases cost and water use [N3-R2]. The recycling evidence indicates that IL recovery can be difficult and that flux can be affected by temperature and IL concentration [N5-R3]. This suggests that toxicity is a concern in conventional solvents, but the evidence does not provide direct toxicity data for all ILs used in pretreatment. In practice, therefore, the major limitations are cost, water use, and recycling challenges, with toxicity being a broader environmental concern rather than a directly measured limitation in the provided evidence [N1-F1][N3-R2][N5-R3].

### Bottom line

Ionic liquids pretreat cellulose-containing lignocellulosic materials by disrupting lignin–cellulose interactions, swelling cellulose, and dissolving lignocellulosic components. The most commonly used systems are 1-alkyl-3-methylimidazolium-based ILs, with [Bmim][Cl], [Emim][Ac], [Bmim][BF4], [Bmim]Ac, and [Bmim][HSCH2CO2] appearing repeatedly in the evidence [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5]. Typical outcomes are improved sugar release, increased saccharification yield, and enhanced lignin recovery [N3-R3][N6-R3][N6-R5]. However, the evidence does not provide a single representative yield figure, so the reported results are best described as generally favorable compared with untreated or less effective pretreatments [N3-R3][N6-R3][N6-R5].

The practical trade-offs are significant: while IL pretreatment can improve yield and recovery, it also faces cost, water-use, and recycling challenges [N1-F1][N3-R2][N5-R3]. Common ionic liquid systems and their practical roles in pretreatment

The evidence points to a family of water-miscible and cellulose-dissolving ILs as the most commonly used systems for lignocellulosic pretreatment. Why certain ILs are preferred over others for lignocellulosic materials
The preference for specific ILs is tied to their physicochemical properties and their ability to dissolve or swell biomass. The review states that ILs are “highly polar” and have “enhanced biopolymer dissolving capacity” [N2-R4], which is important because lignocellulosic biomass is a rigid, crosslinked composite of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin [N1-F1]. In other words, the anion is often more important than the cation for dissolution, while the cation can be tuned to balance solubility with processability [N2-R5][N1-F1].

The evidence suggests that IL pretreatment improves cellulose accessibility by disrupting lignin-cellulose interactions and by swelling cellulose. The review states that ILs can dissolve lignocellulosic materials including crystalline cellulose and that pretreatment can help reduce the recalcitrance of the lignin–carbohydrate complex [N1-F1]. Mechanism and process of ionic liquid pretreatment of lignocellulosic materials

The evidence supports a mechanism in which ionic liquids disrupt lignin-cellulose interactions by weakening the lignin–carbohydrate complex and breaking hydrogen bonds and covalent crosslinks. The review explicitly states that lignocellulosic biomass requires pretreatment to reduce recalcitrance, which entails breaking hydrogen bonds in crystalline cellulose and covalent crosslinks in lignin, as well as removing hemicelluloses [N1-F1]. It also states that ILs can dissolve lignocellulosic materials including crystalline cellulose [N1-F1]. This indicates that the primary mechanism is not just solvation but also structural disruption of the biomass matrix. The review further describes ILs as “unique green alternatives” to hazardous conventional solvents and notes that their physicochemical properties can be adjusted by selecting an appropriate cation–anion combination [N1-F1]. This supports the idea that ILs are chosen not only for their dissolution ability but also for their tunable properties.

Cellulose swelling and solvation effects
The evidence is strongest on the swelling and solvation effects of ILs. The review states that ILs have “enhanced biopolymer dissolving capacity” and that they can dissolve lignocellulosic materials including crystalline cellulose [N2-R4][N1-F1]. Another search result indicates that ILs such as [Bmim]Ac and [Bmim][HSCH2CO2] are especially efficient solvents for microcrystalline cellulose [N2-R5]. This suggests that cellulose swelling and solvation are significant effects of IL pretreatment. However, the evidence does not provide detailed mechanistic details on how swelling occurs, so the claim should be framed as supported by the reported dissolution behavior rather than by a fully resolved molecular mechanism [N2-R5][N1-F1].

How pretreatment conditions influence material separation and recovery
The evidence on process conditions is indirect but still informative. The review emphasizes that the optimum operating conditions for dissolution are commented on and that process parameters are important for industrial use [N1-F1]. For material separation and recovery, the evidence on downstream recovery is more relevant than on pretreatment conditions per se. The evidence on IL recovery and recycling notes that small drops of the new liquid phase can be observed and that the IL phase can be separated by sedimentation after 2 days [N5-R1]. It also indicates that IL recovery is a major concern in biorefinery processes, with a technoeconomic analysis showing that an extensive water washing step is necessary and that this increases cost and water use [N3-R2][N5-R2]. Taken together, these points imply that pretreatment conditions such as temperature, IL concentration, and water washing influence both the effectiveness of pretreatment and the ease of separating and recovering ILs and biomass components [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3].

In summary, ionic liquid pretreatment disrupts lignin-cellulose interactions by weakening the lignin–carbohydrate complex, breaking hydrogen bonds, and covalent crosslinks, and by dissolving crystalline cellulose [N1-F1][N2-R4]. The process also causes swelling and solvation effects, with cellulose dissolution and microcrystalline cellulose solubility being especially important [N2-R5]. Pretreatment conditions influence separation and recovery because higher IL concentrations and temperature can improve separation, while water washing and recycling challenges make recovery difficult and costly [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3].

Major limitations such as cost, toxicity, and recycling challenges

The evidence shows that process parameters interact in ways that affect both yield and operability. The evidence shows that multiple efficiency metrics are used, including saccharification yield, enzyme hydrolysis rate, and lignin recovery [N3-R3][N6-R3][N6-R5]. The review also notes that the optimum operating conditions for the dissolution process are commented on and that IL properties can be adjusted by cation–anion combination [N1-F1]. The recovery evidence further indicates that water washing is necessary and that this increases cost and water use [N3-R2]. The recycling evidence adds that IL recovery can be affected by temperature and IL concentration [N5-R3]. These differences in metrics and results are explained by the fact that pretreatment efficiency depends on the target product—whether the focus is on sugars, lignin, or biomass fractionation—and on the process conditions used [N3-R3][N1-F1][N5-R3].

### Practical constraints and trade-offs

Major limitations of IL pretreatment include cost, water use, and recycling challenges. The review emphasizes that synthesis costs and economic hurdles are important challenges for industrial use [N1-F1]. The recovery evidence notes that an extensive water washing step is necessary, which increases cost and water use [N3-R2]. The recycling evidence indicates that IL recovery can be difficult and that flux can be affected by temperature and IL concentration [N5-R3]. While the evidence does not directly quantify toxicity, it does position ILs as “green” alternatives to hazardous conventional volatile organic solvents [N1-F1]. This suggests that toxicity is a concern in conventional solvents, but the evidence does not provide direct toxicity data for all ILs used in pretreatment. In practice, therefore, the major limitations are cost, water use, and recycling challenges, with toxicity being a broader environmental concern rather than a directly measured limitation in the provided evidence [N1-F1][N3-R2][N5-R3].

Process parameters interact in ways that affect both yield and operability. Temperature and time are important: higher temperature and longer time can improve IL diffusion and pretreatment effectiveness [N4-R2], but they may also reduce reducing sugar yield during pretreatment [N4-R1]. IL concentration also matters: higher concentration can improve dissolution and recovery, but it can also increase operational complexity and water use [N5-R3][N4-R1]. Moisture content and lignin content are mentioned as factors influencing pretreatment efficiency [N4-R4]. Taken together, these parameters suggest that optimizing yield requires careful control of temperature, time, IL concentration, and moisture content, while operability is affected by the need for water washing, separation, and recycling [N4-R1][N4-R2][N5-R3][N4-R4].

Downstream processing needs are substantial. The recovery evidence notes that extensive water washing is required [N3-R2], which implies a need for efficient washing and separation. The recycling evidence notes that IL recovery can be separated by sedimentation after 2 days and that flux is affected by temperature and IL concentration [N5-R1][N5-R3]. The review also emphasizes that process conditions must be optimized for industrial use, including recovery and recycling [N1-F1]. In addition, the comparison context suggests that downstream processing must align with the target product, because IL pretreatment can be used to improve sugar release, lignin recovery, or biomass fractionation [N3-R3][N6-R3]. Therefore, downstream processing needs include water washing, IL recovery, separation, and possibly further fractionation or regeneration steps [N3-R2][N5-R1][N5-R3][N1-F1].

### Bottom line

Ionic liquids pretreat cellulose-containing lignocellulosic materials by disrupting lignin–cellulose interactions, swelling cellulose, and dissolving lignocellulosic components. The most commonly used systems are 1-alkyl-3-methylimidazolium-based ILs, with [Bmim][Cl], [Emim][Ac], [Bmim][BF4], [Bmim]Ac, and [Bmim][HSCH2CO2] appearing repeatedly in the evidence [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5]. Typical outcomes are improved sugar release, increased saccharification yield, and enhanced lignin recovery [N3-R3][N6-R3][N6-R5]. However, the evidence does not provide a single representative yield figure, so the reported results are best described as generally favorable compared with untreated or less effective pretreatments [N3-R3][N6-R3][N6-R5].

The practical trade-offs are significant: while IL pretreatment can improve yield and recovery, it also faces cost, water-use, and recycling challenges [N1-F1][N3-R2][N5-R3]. Process parameters such as temperature, time, IL concentration, and moisture content must be carefully balanced to optimize yield versus operability [N4-R1][N4-R2][N5-R3][N4-R4]. Downstream processing therefore requires water washing, IL recovery, separation, and sometimes further fractionation [N3-R2][N5-R1][N5-R3][N1-F1].
